name: Outcome bias
statement: People judge a decision by how it turned out, rating the same choice as better thinking when the result was good than when it was bad.
meaning: The claim is narrower than it first looks. Nobody disputes that a bad result is often a clue that a decision was bad, and Baron and Hershey grant that outcomes are worth reading when the actor knew things the judge does not. Their bias is what happens once that reason is removed. Judges are handed every probability the decision maker had, told the decision maker had nothing more, and then told the ending. On those terms the ending carries no information about the quality of the thinking, and ratings move anyway. The effect shows up on three separate measures: how good the thinking was, how competent the decision maker is, and whether the judge would let that person decide on their behalf. Asked directly, most judges say outcomes should not count.

origin.who: Jonathan Baron and John C. Hershey
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Five studies at the University of Pennsylvania. Four used medical cases, one used monetary gambles and the last used two decks of cards. The lead case gave a 55-year-old man with chest pain a bypass operation that would raise his life expectancy from age 65 to age 70, with 8% of patients dying from the operation itself. Half the cases ended in success and half in failure. The 8% was chosen from pilot data to make the decision look difficult to the subjects.

evidence: Experiment 1 gave 20 Pennsylvania undergraduates 15 medical decisions on a scale from +3 for clearly correct to -3 for incorrect and inexcusable, with the instruction to rate the thinking that went into the decision. Cases with a good ending scored 0.70 higher than the matched cases with a bad ending, t(19) = 4.04, p < .001 one-tailed. The shift came from a minority of judgements: across 140 pairs differing only in ending, 44.3% favoured the success case, 9.3% favoured the failure case and 46.4% were rated equal. The pattern held where the patient rather than the physician made the choice, mean 0.48, t(19) = 2.59, p < .01. Baron and Hershey note in a footnote that the effect looked larger for physician decisions, mean 0.80, and that the gap between the two was itself marginal, t(19) = 2.04, p = .05 two-tailed. Seven of the last eight participants said outcomes should not count, and those seven showed the effect, t(6) = 3.26, p < .01. Experiment 2 gave 41 people a 30 to -30 scale and kept three sets of cases apart: physician surgery, mean 4.97, t(38) = 3.15, p < .005; patient surgery, mean 4.15, t(40) = 2.21, p < .025; and testing decisions, mean 3.50, t(40) = 3.80, p < .001. Experiment 3 moved 40 people to 16 monetary gambles resolved by a fair roulette wheel. The winning gamble was rated 9.91 points higher, t(39) = 5.40, p < .001. Decisions also scored higher when the road not taken turned out badly, mean 5.03, t(38) = 4.15, p < .001. Experiment 4 ran 29 people, who rated the decision and then predicted the physician's future competence on a 0 to 100 scale anchored on the most and least competent physician in the country. Decision ratings moved by 2.90, t(28) = 2.10, p < .025. Competence ratings moved by 3.41, t(24) = 2.26, p < .025, on the 25 participants whose competence ratings were kept after four were excluded for saying outcome should count. Experiment 5 dropped the within-subject design. Its 111 students, drawn from the first author's own class in thinking and decision making, were more willing to let another student decide a gamble on their behalf after that student had won. Baron and Hershey report the two orders separately, p < .005 two-tailed where the mystery deck was chosen first and p < .01 where the ordinary deck was, both by Fisher's exact test. Two studies find the same thing in doctors judging care. Caplan, Posner and Cheney asked 112 practising anaesthesiologists to judge 21 cases of adverse anaesthetic outcomes, each paired with an alternate version identical but for an outcome of opposite severity. The two sets were split between reviewers who were blind to the study's intent, so nobody saw both versions of a case. Ratings of appropriate care fell by 31 percentage points when a temporary outcome was swapped for a permanent one, and rose by 28 points on the reverse swap, with the inverse relation present in 15 of the 21 matched pairs. Plaum and colleagues randomised outcome information in vignettes sent to 191 Dutch emergency physicians and general practitioners, reusing four cases from an earlier American study by Gupta and colleagues. Each vignette ended well, badly, or with the outcome withheld. Care in the abdominal pain case was called adequate by 44% of those told the patient did badly, against 84% given no ending and 88% told the patient did well. The trauma case ran 9%, 31% and 43%, and the chest pain case 5%, 8% and 24%, all p < 0.01. The headache case, written to be of excellent quality, moved not at all, p = 0.60 on the adequate-care measure and p = 0.80 on the Likert ratings behind it.

replication.headline: A preregistered replication with 692 people found the effect larger than the original, and present in those who said outcomes should not count.
replication.detail: Aiyer, Kam, Ng, Young, Shi and Feldman ran conditions 1 to 4 of Baron and Hershey's Experiment 1 as a between-participants 2 x 2, decision maker crossed with outcome, on 692 people recruited through CloudResearch from Amazon Mechanical Turk. Where the physician chose, the success version was rated d = 1.10, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.26 above the failure version; where the patient chose, d = 0.77, 0.62 to 0.93. Both sit above the figures Aiyer and colleagues calculated for the original, 0.53, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.99 for the physician and 0.21, -0.23 to 0.66 for the patient, neither of which Baron and Hershey printed. The replication team warn that a paired d and an independent d are not the same quantity, so the comparison should be read with care. Switching to a between-participants design was the point: it removes the possibility that people rated matched cases alike only because they remembered their earlier answers, which many participants in the original said they were doing. The 44 people who rated the outcome as unimportant still showed the effect, a mean difference of 0.75, 95% CI 0.21 to 1.08, t(38.64) = 2.23, p = .03, Cohen's d = 0.64. A preregistered extension found the good ending also raised how responsible the decision maker was held to be, 6.01 against 5.51, F(1, 688) = 32.36, p < .001. That is the opposite of the direction the team had registered. An exploratory analysis found the good ending raised what participants took the social norm to be, 4.04 against 3.78, F(1, 688) = 21.54, p < .001.

study.cite: Aiyer, S., Kam, H. C., Ng, K. Y., Young, N. A., Shi, J., & Feldman, G. (2023). Outcomes affect evaluations of decision quality: Replication and extensions of Baron and Hershey's (1988) outcome bias Experiment 1. International Review of Social Psychology, 36(1), 12.

limits: No meta-analysis of outcome bias was located. Crossref, Europe PMC, PubMed, FORRT's FLoRA replication atlas entry for the Baron and Hershey DOI and the open web were searched on 21 September 2026. They returned meta-analyses of outcome reporting bias, which is a different thing, and nothing pooling decision-evaluation studies. OpenAlex could not be queried, because the shared free budget for this network address was exhausted. The FLoRA atlas records one replication of the 1988 paper and codes its outcome successful. The absence is a search result, not a verdict. The original effect sizes were calculated by the replication team rather than printed in 1988, and their Table 7 was read directly this time, which settles the lower bound of the physician interval at 0.06. Sample provenance in the original is thin: 20 to 111 undergraduates per study, all at one university, and Experiment 5 used the first author's own class. The replication ran at one site through an online panel and used four of the original 15 cases, one medical scenario. Caplan and colleagues remain read in abstract only at PubMed, so the 31 and 28 point figures are quoted from that abstract and the analysis behind them was not seen; the JAMA article is closed access with no open deposit recorded. Gupta and colleagues, whose vignettes Plaum reused, is closed access too and is described here only as Plaum describes it. Sezer, Zhang, Gino and Bazerman's 2016 paper is closed access at Elsevier. A manuscript of it sits on a co-author's university page, but that draft carries Michael Norton as fourth author where the published record carries Bazerman, and it runs to eight pages of front matter, so no figure from it is reported. Hershey and Baron returned to the question twice, in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes in 1992 and again in 1995 replying to a comment by Raanan Lipshitz. Both are behind the same Elsevier block described below, so they are named as existing and nothing is reported from them.
misreadings: Outcome bias is not hindsight bias, and Baron and Hershey built the studies to keep them apart. Hindsight bias works on judged probability, so that a known ending looks like it was always likely, and has its own record at entry 48. Outcome bias is a direct effect on the verdict, and it survives when the judge is handed the probabilities and told the decision maker had nothing else. Papers that study both are easy to misread. Kneer and Skoczen's title names outcome effects, moral luck and the hindsight bias together, but their ten experiments judge negligence and culpability after a harmful ending, not the quality of a decision taken under stated odds. Their findings belong to entry 119 and are set out there. The size of the thing is also routinely overstated. In Experiment 1 the two endings drew equal ratings in 46.4% of pairs, and in Experiment 4 the competence ratings were equal in 62.0% of pairs. Most judges do not flip; enough shift to move the mean. Knowing about the bias is not a defence. Participants who said the outcome should not count showed the effect in 1988 and again in 2023, and four of the eight participants Baron and Hershey questioned insisted they had not been swayed while their own ratings moved by 0.43, 0.29, 1.43 and 0.71. One direction is worth watching. Where moral luck predicts that a bad ending draws more responsibility, the 2023 replication found the good ending drew more, against its own registered prediction. The moral version, where a careless act is blamed more heavily when it happens to cause harm, is entry 119.

Read in full from the Europe PMC text.

Kneer, M., & Skoczen, I. (2023). Outcome effects, moral luck and the hindsight bias. Cognition, 232, 105258. Read in abstract only at PubMed on 21 September 2026. The published version is indexed as hybrid open access under CC BY, but ScienceDirect and the DOI redirect both answered HTTP 403 with a bot-block page carrying Elsevier's text and data mining reservation, which is not a paywall. The Zurich repository copy sits behind an Anubis proof-of-work challenge whose pass-challenge endpoint answered 'Internal Server Error: administrator has misconfigured Anubis'. The Jagiellonian repository reset the connection on every attempt. PhilArchive, PhilPapers and SSRN each answered HTTP 403. Both repository copies are in any case indexed as submitted versions.

Sezer, O., Zhang, T., Gino, F., & Bazerman, M. H. (2016). Overcoming the outcome bias: Making intentions matter. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 137, 13-26. Closed access at Elsevier, with no open deposit recorded. A manuscript on a co-author's university page was read, but it names a different fourth author and holds only front matter, so nothing is reported from it.

Hershey, J. C., & Baron, J. (1992). Judgment by outcomes: When is it justified? Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 53(1), 89-93. Named as existing, from the Crossref record; the article was not obtained and nothing is reported from it.
